1. Explain why Bessel’s correction (dividing by n − 1) is an application of the unbiasedness property.

An estimator is unbiased if its average over all possible samples equals the parameter. Dividing the sum of squared deviations by n gives a variance whose average is only (n − 1)/n × σ², because deviations are measured from x̄, which sits closer to the data than μ does. Dividing by n − 1 instead scales the average up to exactly σ². The correction exists to make s² unbiased.

2. For today’s 30 weights, s² = 3.07 kg². What is the divide-by-n variance, and in which direction is it biased?

Divide-by-n variance = 3.07 × 29/30 = 2.97 kg². It is biased downwards: on average it underestimates σ² by the factor 29/30. The bias shrinks as n grows, so the estimator is consistent.

3. A point estimate alone is called incomplete. What is missing from it?

Any statement of precision: how far the estimate might plausibly be from the parameter. A confidence interval supplies it.

1. A colleague says, “There is a 95% probability that the true mean lies in this interval.” Correct the statement.

The true mean is fixed; the computed interval either contains it or does not. The 95% describes the procedure: if sampling and interval construction were repeated many times, about 95% of the intervals would contain the true mean.

2. For today’s 30 children (x̄ = 11.81 kg, SE = 0.32 kg, t₂₉ for 99% = 2.756), compute the 99% CI. Is it wider or narrower than the 95% CI, and why?

Margin = 2.756 × 0.32 = 0.88 kg. 99% CI = 11.81 ± 0.88 = 10.93 to 12.69 kg. It is wider than the 95% CI (11.16 to 12.47 kg) because capturing μ more often requires going further into the tails: 2.756 > 2.045.

3. Two independent groups of 50 each have SD 2 kg and means differing by 0.8 kg. Compute SE_diff and the 95% CI for the difference. Does it include 0?

SE_diff = √(2²/50 + 2²/50) = √(0.08 + 0.08) = √0.16 = 0.40 kg. 95% CI = 0.8 ± 1.96 × 0.40 = 0.8 ± 0.78 = 0.02 to 1.58 kg. It just excludes 0, so the data are incompatible with a zero difference at the 5% level, though the lower limit shows the true difference could be very small.

1. Two of 25 children in an anganwadi test positive for a condition. Compute the Wald 95% CI and state what is wrong with it. Which intervals would you report instead?

p̂ = 2/25 = 0.08. SE = √(0.08 × 0.92/25) = 0.054. Wald CI = 0.08 ± 1.96 × 0.054 = −2.6% to 18.6%. The lower limit is an impossible negative proportion; with np̂ = 2 the Normal approximation fails. Report the Wilson interval (2.2% to 25.0%) or the Clopper–Pearson exact interval (1.0% to 26.0%).

2. A surgeon reports “no wound infections in 60 caesarean sections”. Using the rule of three, what infection risk is still compatible with this record?

Upper 95% limit ≈ 3/60 = 0.05. A true infection risk as high as 5% is compatible with zero infections in 60 operations. (Exact one-sided limit: 1 − 0.05^(1/60) = 4.9%.)

3. For n = 50, P(X ≤ 17) = 0.016 and P(X ≤ 18) = 0.032 for X ~ Binomial(50, 0.5). Which ordered values form the 95% CI for the median?

Choose r so that P(X ≤ r − 1) ≤ 0.025. P(X ≤ 17) = 0.016 qualifies but P(X ≤ 18) = 0.032 does not, so r − 1 = 17 and r = 18. The upper rank is n + 1 − r = 51 − 18 = 33. The CI runs from the 18th to the 33rd ordered value, with coverage 1 − 2 × 0.016 = 96.7%.

1. You want to halve the margin of error of a planned prevalence survey. Roughly how much larger must the sample be, and why?

Four times larger. n = Z²p(1 − p)/d², so n ∝ 1/d². Halving d multiplies n by 2² = 4, because the standard error shrinks only with √n.

2. Expected anaemia prevalence among adolescent girls is 10%, with a margin of ±3 percentage points at 95% confidence. Compute n₀. Then adjust for a cluster design with DEFF = 2 and 85% expected response.

n₀ = 1.96² × 0.10 × 0.90/0.03² = 3.8416 × 0.09/0.0009 = 384.2. With the design effect: 384.2 × 2 = 768.3. With non-response: 768.3/0.85 = 903.9, so approach 904 girls.

3. For the same 10%, what n₀ is needed for a relative precision of ±20%? Why is it larger than in question 2?

d = 0.20 × 0.10 = 0.02. n₀ = Z²q/(ε²p) = 3.8416 × 0.90/(0.04 × 0.10) = 864.4 → 865. It is larger because ±20% of 10% is ±2 points, a tighter margin than the ±3 points of question 2.

1. A block with a mid-year population of 60,000 registers 1,500 live births, 42 infant deaths (27 of them neonatal), 25 stillbirths, 18 early neonatal deaths and 3 maternal deaths. Compute the CBR, IMR, NMR, PMR and MMR.

  • CBR = 1,500/60,000 × 1,000 = 25 per 1,000 population.
  • IMR = 42/1,500 × 1,000 = 28 per 1,000 live births.
  • NMR = 27/1,500 × 1,000 = 18 per 1,000 live births.
  • PMR = (25 + 18)/(1,500 + 25) × 1,000 = 43/1,525 × 1,000 = 28.2 per 1,000 births (the denominator includes stillbirths).
  • MMR = 3/1,500 × 100,000 = 200 per 100,000 live births.

2. Why is the case fatality rate not a rate, and why can it mislead early in an outbreak?

It is a proportion (deaths among cases ÷ cases) with no time component, so it measures severity, not a rate of occurrence. Early in an outbreak, detected cases are skewed towards severe ones (inflating it), and some current cases have not yet died or recovered (deflating it).

3. Diabetes has a prevalence of 10% in a town, and people live with it for an average of 20 years. Assuming a steady state, what is the approximate annual incidence among people without diabetes?

P/(1 − P) = I × D, so 0.10/0.90 = 0.111 = I × 20, giving I = 0.0056 per year, about 5.6 new cases per 1,000 people without diabetes per year. The shortcut P ≈ I × D gives 0.10/20 = 5 per 1,000; it underestimates here because a prevalence of 10% is not small.

1. Two districts have age-specific death rates of 2 and 20 per 1,000 (District X) and 3 and 24 per 1,000 (District Y) in the under-60 and 60+ groups. Using a standard population of 60,000 under-60 and 40,000 aged 60+, compute both DSRs.

X: expected deaths in the standard = 2 × 60 + 20 × 40 = 120 + 800 = 920; DSR = 920/100,000 × 1,000 = 9.2 per 1,000. Y: 3 × 60 + 24 × 40 = 180 + 960 = 1,140; DSR = 11.4 per 1,000. Y’s standardised mortality is 11.4/9.2 = 1.24 times X’s.

2. A PHC catchment records 30 deaths where 20 were expected at state rates. Compute the SMR and its approximate 95% CI. What do you conclude?

SMR = 30/20 = 1.5. SE(ln SMR) = 1/√30 = 0.183. CI = 1.5 × exp(± 1.96 × 0.183) = 1.5 × exp(± 0.358) = 1.05 to 2.15 (exact Poisson: 1.01 to 2.14). Mortality is about 50% above what state rates predict for this age structure; the interval excludes 1, but with only 30 deaths the excess could be anywhere from a few per cent to more than double.

3. Why is indirect rather than direct standardisation used for a small PHC catchment?

Direct standardisation needs the catchment’s own age-specific death rates, which rest on very few deaths per age group and are unstable. Indirect standardisation needs only the catchment’s age structure and total deaths, borrowing stable age-specific rates from the standard (state) population.

1. In a 5-year band, the death rate is 0.02 per person-year and those who die live on average 2.5 years in the band. Compute ₅qₓ.

₅qₓ = n × M/[1 + (n − a) × M] = 5 × 0.02/(1 + 2.5 × 0.02) = 0.10/1.05 = 0.095.

2. Using the table above, what is the probability that a 15-year-old survives to age 45?

l₄₅/l₁₅ = 89,161/95,388 = 0.935 (93.5%).

3. If the open 60+ band had a death rate of 0.05 per person-year, what would e₆₀ be? Why can e₁ exceed e₀?

e₆₀ = 1/M = 1/0.05 = 20 years. e₁ can exceed e₀ because e₀ averages over everyone born, including the many who die in infancy; a child who survives the first year has passed that high-risk period, so its expected remaining life can be longer than a newborn’s (here 68.8 vs 67.7 years).
